definition.text: Aldo Leopold (1887–1948) was an American forester, ecologist, writer and conservationist, known for his land ethic.

facts.text: His land ethic widens the idea of community to include soils, waters, plants and animals, together called the land.
He described conservation as a state of harmony between people and land, in his posthumous 1949 book A Sand County Almanac.
His 1933 book Game Management helped found wildlife management as a science and was its leading textbook for over 40 years.
In 1921 he argued for preserving roadless wilderness in national forests, proposing the Gila headwaters as a prime case.

title: Garrett Hardin

definition.text: Garrett Hardin (1915–2003) was an American ecologist and microbiologist, best known for his 1968 paper "The Tragedy of the Commons".

facts.text: His 1968 Science paper drew attention to the damage that innocent individual actions can do to the environment.
The essay drew on an 1833 pamphlet by William Forster Lloyd about herders overgrazing a shared parcel of land.
He applied the model to population growth, natural resource use and the welfare state, writing that freedom in a commons brings ruin to all.
Critics said he ignored the demographic transition and confused common property with open-access resources, and Elinor Ostrom's work contradicted his pessimism.
His First Law of Human Ecology holds that we can never do just one thing, since any intrusion into nature has many unpredictable effects.
His hardline positions on immigration, race and eugenics have led several sources to label him a white nationalist.

contested_note: His tragedy-of-the-commons argument is disputed by critics and contradicted by Ostrom's field studies of successful commons.
